content.text:
Fixed and verified. I ended up writing the predicate rather than leaving you a stub — a `todo!()` would have failed `-D warnings` on unused params, and it seemed better to hand you something working with the one judgment call marked than something that doesn't compile.

## The predicate

[oauth_consent.rs:244](crates/pds/src/routes/oauth_consent.rs:244) — a handle binds only when **both** halves of the atproto bidirectional rule hold:

```rust
if !authority.asserts_handle(&handle) { return Ok(false); }              // the account claims it
Ok(resolve_handle_to_did(state, &handle).await?.as_deref() == Some(did)) // …and it resolves back
```

**This is the line you may want to change.** Dropping the second check would remove a DNS lookup from the approve path, but `alsoKnownAs` is writable by whoever controls a DID — so any account could claim `malpercio.dev` and approve a request named for you. The client would still learn the real DID from the token's `sub`, so it's narrow, but it defeats the binding's purpose entirely. I kept it. One-line change if you disagree.

## Where the check moved, and why

It was step 3 (before signature verification); it's now step 6, after `authority.authorizes()`. Two reasons: the authoritative `alsoKnownAs` only exists once step 5 has fetched it, and putting handle resolution behind the authorization check means only a genuine key holder can drive that outbound lookup.

`AuthoritySet` now carries the handles alongside the keys, read from the same authoritative fetch both branches already performed — [authority.rs](crates/pds/src/identity/authority.rs). No new network call for the assertion half; the PLC audit log and the live did:web document both already contained it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Placing the binding after `authorizes()` inverts the usual "cheap checks first" instinct, and deliberately. The old ordering was cheap-first, which is why a *string comparison* got to reject before a *cryptographic proof* was examined — and why the wallet's error copy blamed the keys for a decision made before the keys were consulted. Ordering by cost rather than by authority is what let a weak check overrule a strong one.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Verification

I proved the tests are load-bearing rather than trusting a green run: temporarily restoring `hint == did` made the two binding tests fail with `left: 401, right: 200` — your exact production symptom — while the three rejection tests stayed green. Then reverted.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo test -p pds` | 2283 passed, 0 failed |
| `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| ticket-ref / changelog / auth-seam / bruno-parity | all pass |

Four tests added: handle binds, `@Owner.Example.com` normalizes and binds, asserted-but-unresolvable rejected, never-asserted rejected.

## Two things to note

**Scope is wider than your account.** This broke wallet consent for *every* account on Custos, both DID methods, against any client that forwards a `login_hint` — which is most of them. `rpg.actor` isn't special.

**A residual sharp edge.** `resolve_handle_to_did` reports a DNS/well-known outage as `Ok(None)`, not an error, so during a resolution outage a user-domain handle is refused rather than 502-ing. Entering the DID still works (that path does no resolution). I documented it on the function rather than papering over it — changing it means teaching the resolution chain to distinguish "not found" from "couldn't ask", which is a larger change than this fix.

Nothing is committed. Linear's MCP needs authorization that I can't complete in this non-interactive session, so I used a descriptive changelog slug (`oauth-consent-login-hint.fixed.md`) rather than inventing an MM number — worth filing an issue and renaming if you want the traceability. Want me to commit and open a PR?

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" && gh pr create --base main --head claude/oauth-signature-verification-086959 --title "Bind a handle-shaped OAuth consent login_hint to the account it names" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## What happened

Signing in to a third-party app (`rpg.actor`) with a wallet-confirmed OAuth consent failed with:

> **Your server rejected the approval** — The signature could not be verified against your identity's current keys. Nothing was granted.

The signature was fine. So were the keys. The request was rejected two steps earlier.

`POST /oauth/authorize/approve` runs in this order:

```
step 3  → account binding: login_hint must equal the approving DID   ← failed here
step 5  → verify envelope signature + authoritative key lookup        ← never reached
```

Both return the same opaque `approval_rejected()` (deliberately — the surface must not leak which check failed), the wallet maps its 401 to `APPROVAL_REJECTED`, and that code renders the "signature could not be verified" copy. So the one branch that cannot possibly be about signatures is the branch that reports a signature failure.

The check itself:

```rust
if let Some(hint) = pending.login_hint.as_deref() {
    if hint != request.did { return Err(approval_rejected()); }
}
```

`login_hint` is stored **verbatim and never resolved** — `oauth_par.rs` only filters empties, `oauth_authorize.rs` copies it straight into the pending row (its own comment notes the value is unverified and may be a handle or an attacker-chosen DID). atproto clients forward whatever the user typed, which is a handle. So the comparison was:

```
"malpercio.dev"  !=  "did:web:malpercio.dev"   → rejected
```

**Confirmed empirically:** the consent page showed `malpercio.dev` pre-filled in its identifier field (it pre-populates from `login_hint`). Re-running the flow with the DID typed instead succeeded.

## Scope

Not specific to one account or DID method. This broke wallet-confirmed consent for **every** account on Custos against **any** client that forwards a `login_hint`, which is most of them. It only ever worked for clients that omit the hint or happen to send a raw DID — which is also why the existing test suite missed it: `login_hint_mismatch_is_rejected` only covered a DID-shaped hint.

## The fix

A handle binds only when **both** halves of the atproto bidirectional rule hold:

```rust
if !authority.asserts_handle(&handle) { return Ok(false); }              // the account claims it
Ok(resolve_handle_to_did(state, &handle).await?.as_deref() == Some(did)) // …and it resolves back
```

Assertion alone is the account's own claim — `alsoKnownAs` is writable by whoever controls the DID, so requiring only that would let any account claim any handle and approve a request named for someone else. The client would still learn the real DID from the token's `sub`, so the gap is narrow, but it defeats the binding's entire purpose.

`AuthoritySet` now carries the asserted handles alongside the signing keys, populated from the **same authoritative fetch both branches already performed** — the PLC audit log for did:plc, the live document for did:web — never the `did_documents` cache (which a Custos-hosted did:web account can rewrite under session auth). The assertion half therefore costs no additional request.

DID-shaped hints keep exact-match behaviour. Handles are normalized for `at://` / `@` / ASCII case first, since clients forward what the user typed.

## Why the check moved

From step 3 to step 6, after `authorizes()`. Two reasons: the authoritative `alsoKnownAs` only exists once step 5 has fetched it, and sitting behind the authorization check means only a genuine key holder can drive the outbound handle resolution.

This inverts the usual cheap-checks-first instinct, on purpose. Cost-ordering is exactly what let a string comparison reject a request before a cryptographic proof was examined — and why the error blamed the keys for a decision made before the keys were consulted.

## Verification

The new tests were proven load-bearing rather than trusted green: temporarily restoring `hint == did` made the two binding tests fail with `left: 401, right: 200` — the reported production symptom — while the three rejection tests stayed green. Then reverted.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/jacob.zweifel/.claude/skills/pr-review-comments

# Batch PR Review-Comment Triage

Pull every unresolved review thread on the current PR in one command, then triage the batch. The user should never have to paste review comments one at a time.

## Fetch unresolved threads

Determine the PR number for the current branch (`gh pr view --json number -q .number`), then:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){
  repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
    pullRequest(number:$pr){
      reviewThreads(first:100){
        nodes{
          isResolved isOutdated path line
          comments(first:30){nodes{author{login} body url}}
        }
      }
    }
  }
}' -F owner=<owner> -F repo=<repo> -F pr=<number> \
| jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
       | select(.isResolved==false)
       | {path, line, isOutdated,
          comments: [.comments.nodes[] | {author: .author.login, url, body}]}]'
```

Also fetch top-level (non-thread) review bodies and issue comments if the bot posts summaries there:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --json reviews,comments
```

## Triage the batch

For each unresolved thread, classify before fixing anything:

1. **Correctness / security / portability** — verify the claim against the actual code, then fix if real. Automated reviewers assert confidently and are sometimes wrong; refute with evidence when they are.
2. **Legitimate but out of scope** — file a follow-up issue rather than growing the PR.
3. **Pure style nit / preference** — decline with a one-line reason.

Present the full disposition table (thread → classification → action) to the user in ONE message before applying fixes, so they approve the batch rather than each item. Note that every fix-commit re-triggers CI and (for assertive bots like CodeRabbit) a fresh review round that tends to find one more micro-nit — batch fixes into a single commit where possible.

## Resolving threads

After pushing fixes, reply/resolve via:

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='mutation($id:ID!){resolveReviewThread(input:{threadId:$id}){thread{isResolved}}}' -F id=<threadId>
```

(Include `id` in the reviewThreads query above if you plan to resolve threads programmatically.)

input.content: Approving a third-party app's sign-in from Obsign failed with "your server rejected the approval — the signature could not be verified against your identity's current keys" whenever the app passed along the handle you had typed. Custos compared that hint to your DID as plain text, so `alice.example.com` never matched `did:plc:…`, and the approval was refused two steps before your signature was ever examined — the message blamed your keys for something they had not done. Nothing was ever wrong with Obsign's signature or with any account's keys. Custos now binds a handle-shaped hint to the account it actually names, requiring both that the account claims the handle in its DID document and that the handle resolves back to that DID, so neither half alone lets one account approve a request named for another. Handles are matched without regard to case, as the AT Protocol intends. Typing your DID instead of your handle was the workaround and still works — and remains the way through if handle resolution for your domain is down.

content.text:
CodeRabbit flipped to **APPROVED**. Both threads addressed, replied to, and resolved in `c1be69f1`.

## Disposition

| Thread | Classification | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `authority.rs:55` — asserted handles not case-normalized | **Correctness — real** | Fixed |
| `changelog.d/…` — say "Obsign", not "the wallet" | **Convention — real** | Fixed |
| MD041 "first line should be a heading" (tooling noise inside thread 1) | Not applicable | Ignored — fragments are headingless by design |

## The correctness one was genuinely right

I verified before accepting rather than taking the assertion on faith: a test mounting `alsoKnownAs: ["at://Owner.Example.com"]` against a lowercase hint failed `left: 401, right: 200` on the pre-fix code.

`asserted_handles` preserved each alias's original case; `hint_binds_account` lowercased the caller's hint; `asserts_handle` compared them exactly. So an account whose document asserts a mixed-case handle had every legitimate approval refused — **the same silent-rejection class this PR exists to fix, on the other side of the comparison.**

I took the suggested fix (fold in `asserted_handles`) over case-insensitive comparison in `asserts_handle`, so the set is normalized once where it's derived rather than at each caller.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
Worth noting where this bug came from: I normalized the *input* I was thinking about (the hint) and not the *data* I was comparing it against, because the test fixture happened to be lowercase. A fixture that agrees with your assumption can't test it. The general shape — normalize at the boundary where a set is constructed, not at each comparison site — is what keeps the two sides from drifting apart, and it's why the fold belongs in `asserted_handles`.

This is also the second time on this PR that the reachable path was a hand-authored did:web document. `malpercio.dev`'s own `did.json` is a static file behind Caddy, so "the document can carry any case" isn't hypothetical here.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo test -p pds` | 2284 passed, 0 failed (+1 new test) |
| `cargo clippy -p pds --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `changelog-check` / `ticket-ref-check` | pass |
| CodeRabbit / GitGuardian | success |

The PDS gate and CodeQL jobs were still running when I checked. The PR is otherwise green and approved — worth a glance at the PDS gate before you merge, though it runs the same `just ci-pds` steps I ran locally.
